concept.name: Order arrival rate
concept.definition: The frequency per unit time at which new orders of a given type or side reach a trading venue. It is a core primitive of queueing-based microstructure and market-making models - in the Avellaneda-Stoikov lineage formalized by Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013), arrival rates of liquidity-consuming orders depend on the distance of the quote from the reference price.
concept.intuition: It measures how busy the order flow is - how many new orders show up each second at each price.
concept.mechanics: Estimated empirically as counts of order events per interval by side and price level, and modeled as Poisson or self-exciting (Hawkes) intensities; arrival rates jointly determine fill probabilities, queue dynamics, and optimal quote placement.
concept.formula: lambda = N_orders / Dt (orders per unit time); in market-making models, fill intensity lambda(delta) decreases with the distance delta of the quote from the reference price.
concept.failure_modes: Arrival rates are strongly time-varying (U-shaped intraday patterns, news bursts) and clustered, so stationary Poisson calibrations fail out of sample; venue-specific message throttles also truncate observed rates.
concept.misconceptions: A high order arrival rate does not imply high traded volume: in automated markets most messages are small orders that are cancelled before execution.
concept.example: A liquid future sees 500 limit-order submissions per second at the inside prices but only 50 per second three ticks away.

citations.source: Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia, 'Dealing with the Inventory Risk: A Solution to the Market Making Problem', Mathematics and Financial Economics 7(4):477-507 (arXiv preprint)
